answer: Hi everyone, this is Jaden Chow. Welcome to the Shark Tank PHS virtual club space. Today we're answering an important question. What is crucial if you want a VC to fund your business idea? First, what is a VC? VC stands for Venture Capitalist. A VC is someone who gives money to new businesses they believe can grow big. Instead of getting paid back like a loan, they receive part ownership of the business. If the business succeeds, they succeed, too. Because of that, VCs don't invest in just any idea. They invest in ideas that are clear, realistic, and ready to grow. That's where the winning pitch formula comes in. First is the problem. You must clearly explain a real pain point people actually have. Second, the solution. What is your product or service, and how does it work? Third, the value proposition. Why is your solution better or different from others? Fourth, the market. Who is this for, and how many people need it? Fifth, the business model. How does your idea make money? Next is traction. This is proof that people want your idea, like users, sales, or strong interest. Then comes competition. Other solutions exist. Explain who they are, and why your idea can win. Next are financials. You don't need perfect numbers, but you need to show you understand costs and revenue. Then there's the ask. How much money are you asking for, and what are you offering in return? Finally, vision and scale. Show how your idea can grow bigger in the future. If you can clearly explain all 10 of these, a VC is much more likely to listen. Thanks for watching. See you in the next lesson.

answer: This year marks a significant moment for the UNESCO IHP as we celebrate the 30th birthday of ecohydrology at UNESCO and 20 years of UNESCO ecohydrology demonstration sites. Today, we reflect back from foundations of the science in Poland to the current global influence of ecohydrology. Ecohydrology rose to answer the fundamental question of how to deal with ecosystem problems in the aquatic environment. As Professor Zalewski, director of the European Regional Centre for Ecohydrology, realized that environmental protection alone is not enough. Hence, by studying the mechanisms that regulate the environmental processes through the interactions between the biota and the water system, ecohydrology was born. With water as a driver for all life, the protection and resilience against challenges in the current climatic context, such as pollution, scarcity, management, and drought, is essential. Thus, the second part of ecohydrology is finding and implementing solutions. From the design of experiments in laboratories to the implementation of real systems, research in ecohydrology looks for nature-based solutions to tackle different problems worldwide. To highlight successful implementations of NBS based on ecohydrological values at the water basin scale, UNESCO has supported the formation of 66 demonstration sites. These span 36 countries across all six continents and are excellent case studies for the ecohydrological approach to water management. This network has developed thanks to the UNESCO demonstration site program that brings together researchers, local governments, and communities from all across the world. Examples include the ecological engineering of Las Dunas in the Cahuayumac microbasin in Peru, the natural migration and remediation of watersheds and lagoon ecosystem in Ghar El Melh, Tunisia, wastewater treatment wetland system in Asmelabad, Pakistan, and the Birmingham urban ecohydrological urban observatory in the Upper Tame catchment in the United Kingdom. Another key development is the international Ecohydrology & Hydrobiology Journal aimed at increasing understanding of water-biota interplay and how this knowledge can be used for decision-making tools. The scope aims to address the priorities of the international initiatives, such as the Millennium Development Goals and the UNESCO IHP. With 26 volumes, the journal incorporates climate change, water quality, pollution, and sustainability, and the latest developments of ecohydrological understanding. The importance of ecohydrology will continue to grow with the need to reduce consumption and alleviate pressure on the environment as climate change will bring about new water challenges. With water being a key element of all aspects of life, these 30 years mark only the beginning. To continue building a resilient future, we look to the youth of today. The Ecohydrology Youth Network brings together young people and aims to support the engagement and the development of ideas within the ecohydrology field. With over 500 members, the network connects young scientists, promotes ecohydrological solutions, and exchanges ideas. The future of ecohydrology is looking bluer and greener. And on that note, happy 30th anniversary of ecohydrology and 20 years of ecohydrology demonstration sites.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: The perfect 60-second startup pitch. Imagine you step into an elevator with your dream investor. You have exactly 60 seconds before the doors open. Would you know what to say? Most founders make one big mistake. They try to explain everything about their business. The truth is, your goal isn't to close the investment in 60 seconds. It's to make the investor want another conversation. Here's a simple framework that works. First, start with the problem. What pain are you solving? Keep it simple and relatable. If the investor doesn't understand the problem, they won't care about the solution. Next, explain your solution. In one sentence, describe what your company does. Avoid technical jargon or long explanations. If someone outside your industry can't understand it, it's probably too complicated. Then, explain why now. Why is this the right time for your business? Maybe a new technology has made your solution possible. Maybe customer behavior has changed. Maybe the market is growing rapidly. Investors want to know why this opportunity exists today, not 5 years ago. After that, share your traction. You don't need millions in revenue, but you do need evidence that you're making progress. That could be paying customers, user growth, partnerships, pilot programs, or even a growing waitlist. Traction reduces uncertainty and builds confidence. Finally, finish with the opportunity. Don't end by asking for money. Instead, leave the investor wanting to learn more. Give them a reason to schedule a second meeting. Remember, a great pitch doesn't answer every question. It answers just enough to create curiosity. If an investor walks away wanting to know more, you've done your job. The best founders don't overwhelm investors with information. They tell a clear story, communicate confidence, and make their business easy to understand. Because at the end of the day, investors don't invest in the longest pitch, they invest in the clearest one. If you found this video helpful, subscribe to the Pitch Network for more practical advice on fundraising, networking, and building startups that investors want to back.

answer: In 2016, Casey Neistat ended the most-watched daily vlog on the internet at the exact moment it was still growing. 5 million subscribers, over a billion views, revenue climbing every month. He stopped anyway, telling his audience there was nothing left to say through the format. The metrics were screaming reassurance at him. He ignored them. Seth Godin has published something close to 8,000 blog posts. On his own site, he's written that focus groups and informal feedback are a trap. The people you ask are rarely the ones your work is actually for. He built one of the most cited marketing platforms alive by refusing to let outside opinion gate what got published. Jason Fried co-founded Basecamp on the same refusal. In Rework, he and David Heinemeier Hansson call waiting for perfect information a trap with no exit. Decisions don't get safer the longer you sit on them, they just pile up. Basecamp shipped early and often, without waiting for a chorus of yeses first. Three different fields, same move. All three stopped asking if it was okay and started reading the actual result instead. There's a name for what they refused to do. It comes out of three separate, unconnected corners of clinical research that landed on the same finding without meaning to. Paul Salkovskis' 1985 model of health anxiety, James Coyne's 1976 theory of depression, Adam Radomsky's research on what's called checking by proxy in OCD. Different disorders, different decades, same mechanism. Reassurance lowers anxiety immediately, then the anxiety comes back, often stronger, because the uncertainty underneath it was never actually resolved, just rented for a few hours. I call this the certainty debt loop. Every time you ask for reassurance instead of letting the uncertainty sit, you're not paying off the doubt

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: When you walk into a venture capital pitch, you are stepping into a room defined by heavy skepticism. Every word you say and every slide you show is either building a bridge of trust with the people across the table, or giving them another excuse to say no. The reality of fundraising is that you don't actually win these meetings, you survive them. You keep the conversation alive just long enough to earn a second meeting, by systematically identifying and removing every single reason an investor might hesitate. In 2008, Garrett Camp and Travis Kalanick raised a $200,000 seed round using this presentation. That check grew into an operation valued at $140 billion, even though the deck looks like a rough draft. It runs 25 slides long, ignoring modern advice on brevity. It lacks complex financial models, and barely mentions a business plan. On paper, it should have been discarded during the brutal 3-minute skim test that most VCs use to filter their deal flow. The UberCab deck suggests that at the seed stage, the specific sequencing of trust and psychology can be more influential than the quality of the graphic design. Most founders fall into the trap of the McKinsey-style presentation. They lead with dry market sizing, abstract industry jargon, and theoretical frameworks. It is a logical approach that often feels disconnected from the actual problem being solved. Uber used a structure we call the flipped pyramid. Instead of starting with the math, they hooked the audience with raw, relatable frustration first, saving the spreadsheets for later. They avoided transit industry jargon entirely. Instead, they forced investors to recall the shared misery of trying to hail a cab in a major city. They evoked specific visceral pain points: the 45-minute wait times with zero status updates, and that helpless feeling of standing on a street corner in a downpour hoping an empty car might eventually pass by. Only after they established that emotional wound did they introduce the solution. This direct mapping, linking a technological feature like automated dispatch to a specific human frustration, makes the product feel inevitable. Notice the lack of dense text on these slides. By using simple icons as visual anchors, the deck prevents the investor from reading ahead. It forces the founder to remain the primary storyteller in the room.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Over 50 million transactions were analyzed across 1,000 non-profit organizations globally in 2025. So that means that what we're seeing is actual donor behavior, and that's what we're going to talk about today. So what we found in all of this data is this big paradox. The average one-time gift size actually declined by 1% and the average monthly gift size in the US declined by almost 5.5%. Now that can set off some alarm bells, but here's the paradox. Uh conversion rates are rising. Uh recurring enrollment is growing up to 9% and mobile donations crossed uh 50% threshold. Social to recurring conversion doubled in email. Um what does all this mean? Well, I wanted to start by just kind of researching what other paradoxes are out there and are there any similar ones? Uh and forgive the like little history lesson here, but I found this super interesting. Uh there's this thing called the Jevons paradox. Uh back in the 1800s, this guy William Jevons, he noticed that when steam engines were getting much more efficient, right? We like crossed this threshold where steam engines were getting super super efficient. So the hypothesis was, hey, we're going to use less coal. Well, what happened was people didn't use less coal, the tech was so good that there were more and more steam engines. So everybody got a steam engine and total coal use exploded, right? So how does that relate to this? Well, we're seeing the exact same thing in fundraising right now. As the friction of giving goes down, the initial cost of entry is smaller. The volume of committed donors is really booming. And so donors aren't pulling back, they're moving faster, committing a little bit differently. Smaller upfront gifts don't necessarily mean lower donor value. Organizations that are winning in 2026 will build their revenue architecture around how donors are actually giving today. And from what we've seen in this data, it's mobile-first, it's social-driven, and also commitment-led.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hello and welcome to This Week in Review. This is our weekly segment that's designed to highlight a few important developments that you might have missed this week, and we'll talk about what they mean for markets, and, most importantly, the potential impact for investors. To stay up to date with our latest market insights, subscribe to our YouTube channel or visit fisherinvestments.com. Now, let's review what happened this week. First, the Fed meeting. On Wednesday, the Federal Open Market Committee, or FOMC, voted to hold the interest rate steady at 3.5 to 3.75%. This was the fifth straight meeting without an interest rate change. It was also a split decision, and three members voted to hike rates by 25 basis points. Headlines quickly seized on the story of a divided Fed, but we wouldn't really read too much into that. Differing opinions among Fed officials tells us very little about what the committee will do next, and dissenting votes don't make a rate hike more or less likely in the meetings ahead. Some investors may also worry that Chairman Kevin Warsh's decision to step back from so-called forward guidance may make monetary policy harder to predict or less transparent. We see that differently. Central banks can, and often do, change their minds without notice based on changing economic data or fundamentals. So rather than trying to guess their next move, we think investors are better served by keeping their focus on the broader fundamentals driving markets. Central bank decisions are just one of many forces shaping the global economy and capital markets, and while we believe a rate hike would be a mistake, the talk today is of small hikes. And, really importantly, even a hike or two from here would leave policy rates within a range that this bull market has already successfully navigated. Additionally, when we look around the developed world, yield curves remain steep and healthy. For long-term investors, that's perspective worth holding on to.

answer: There's a quiet rebellion happening against the algorithm life, a return to the physical world. Record: This is about creating a record of your life using one-sentence journal entries to capture your notes, actions, moods, and events. These help us become more aware of patterns in our thinking, feeling, and doing that are impacting our lives. Refine: This is about applying any insights we gain from reflection. None of these are bad and they can all be valuable, but they don't represent the whole picture. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: I am presenting our work, towards calibrating prompt tuning of vision-language models. This work focuses on improving the reliability of prompt-tuned CLIP models. Our main goal is not only to improve accuracy, but also to make the model's confidence more trustworthy. Prompt tuning is widely used because it adapts CLIP efficiently without updating the full model. However, most existing methods mainly focus on classification accuracy. In real-world applications, accuracy alone is not enough. A model must also know how confident it should be. If a model gives high confidence to wrong predictions, it becomes risky in areas such as medical imaging, autonomous systems, and safety-critical AI. Therefore, models' predicted confidence should equal to the true likelihood or model predicted accuracy. This will ensure that the model's predicted confidence is calibrated. Post-hoc calibration can adjust confidence after training, but it cannot prevent embedding drift caused during prompt tuning. Our key observation is that prompt tuning creates a dual miscalibration problem. For base classes, the model often becomes underconfident because the logit margins are reduced. For novel classes, the model becomes overconfident because the margins become inflated or unstable. The reliability diagrams and margin analysis show that margin behavior affects base and novel classes differently. Therefore, we need a train-time method that controls both logit margins and text embedding geometry, which preserves CLIP geometry by preventing prompt-induced semantic drift and stabilizes class relations, reducing overconfident wrong predictions, thereby lowering calibration error. To solve this, we propose two complementary losses. First, the mean variance margin loss stabilizes the logit gap between the ground-truth class and the strongest incorrect class. This helps improve confidence separation. Second, the text moment matching loss preserves CLIP's original text embedding geometry by matching the distribution of tuned text embeddings with frozen CLIP embeddings. The total loss combines cross-entropy, margin regularization, and moment matching. Together, they reduce base class underconfidence and novel class overconfidence. Margin loss alone is useful, but it can still create high-confidence wrong predictions, especially on novel classes. This happens because if the model predicts the wrong class, increasing the margin can make that wrong prediction even more confident. Moment matching solves this by preserving semantic geometry. So, margin improves discriminability, while moment matching prevents semantic drift. Their combination gives better calibration, especially for novel classes. We evaluate the method on 11 datasets: ImageNet, Caltech-101, Pets, Cars, Flowers...

I was fortunate to attend the American Society of Hematology meeting this last December in Orlando, Florida, where multiple presentations covering a series of topics in myeloid malignancies were provided. Among them, we presented the results of PARADIGM, a phase 2 randomized study that compared intensive induction chemotherapy to less intensive azacitidine and venetoclax in fit, traditionally induction-eligible patients. The study met its primary endpoint: event-free survival was better for patients who received azacitidine and venetoclax. There were also multiple secondary endpoints that were important. There was also better quality of life and better patient-reported outcomes. This opens the field to potentially introducing less intensive therapies for patients that are traditionally thought to receive intensive chemotherapy, the long-term standard of care in AML, which allows tolerability, safety, but also allows them to move on to curative modalities such as stem cell transplant. There was also a series of presentations on the combination of azacitidine and venetoclax and targeted therapies, such as gilteritinib, the FLT3 inhibitor, as well as multiple menin inhibitors, such as ziftomenib. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hello, everyone. I'm Jiayin Jin from Hangzhou City University. Today, I'm excited to present our CVPR 2024 paper, UltrasoundCLIP: Semantic-Aware Contrastive Pre-training for Ultrasound Image-Text Understanding. Ultrasound is one of the most widely used imaging modalities in clinical practice. However, ultrasound vision-language learning remains under-explored because of heterogeneous diagnostic attributes and weak image-text alignment. To address this problem, we propose a semantic-aware ultrasound vision-language framework, together with a large-scale ultrasound image-text dataset. Unlike natural images, ultrasound images are highly challenging for vision-language learning. First, ultrasound diagnosis involves heterogeneous diagnostic attributes. For the same lesion, radiologists may describe multiple diagnostic attributes, such as echogenicity, margins, internal characteristics, and calcification. Second, ultrasound images from different organs often look visually similar, even though they correspond to completely different anatomical structures and diagnostic semantics. Because ultrasound image-text pairs often exhibit weak semantic alignment, directly applying conventional CLIP-style contrastive learning is insufficient for ultrasound understanding. This motivates the need for semantic-aware ultrasound representation learning. To address these challenges, we first construct US365K, the first large-scale dedicated ultrasound image-text dataset. The dataset contains over 364,000 image-text pairs collected from more than 11,000 clinical cases, spanning diverse organs and pathological findings. More importantly, we introduce UDT, which stands for Unified Ultrasound Diagnostic Taxonomy. UDT standardizes both anatomical hierarchy and ultrasound diagnostic attributes, providing structured semantic knowledge for ultrasound understanding. This taxonomy serves as the semantic foundation of our framework.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hi. My name is Ava from the MAST program. And in this study, we're looking at how aging impacts the small intestinal microbiome and its relationship to gastrointestinal symptoms. We know that small intestinal bacterial overgrowth, or SIBO, becomes more common as people get older. But what we're still unclear about is why. Whether it's driven by an increase in total bacterial load or shifts in the microbial composition, or even both. So our aim in this study is to determine if there's a relationship between aging, absolute small bowel microbial loads, microbial community structure, and gastrointestinal symptom severity. To address this, we analyzed duodenal aspirate samples from subjects in the REIMAGINE study. These were patients undergoing upper endoscopy without colon prep. We grouped subjects by age and used metagenomic sequencing to quantify absolute microbial abundance, so not just relative composition, but actual bacterial load. What we found is total bacterial load increases significantly with age, and the prevalence of SIBO rises as well. At the same time, microbial diversity declines in older age groups. When we looked more closely at microbial composition, we found that key Gram-negative bacteria, particularly Escherichia coli and Klebsiella species, increase progressively with age in patients with SIBO. These changes were consistent and significant across all age groups. Then we looked at how this relates to symptoms. In subjects over the age of 50, those with SIBO reported significantly greater symptom severity, including diarrhea, bloating, and abdominal pain. Importantly, these symptoms were strongly associated with the abundance of specific bacterial groups, such as Escherichia and Fusobacterium, rather than bacterial load alone. And also, in older subjects without SIBO, increased bacterial load did not correlate with symptom severity. So simply having more bacteria isn't enough to explain symptoms. It really depends on the microbial composition. So overall, our findings suggest that aging is associated with increased bacterial load and reduced diversity, but symptom severity in older adults is more closely linked to specific microbial signatures rather than total load alone. This highlights the importance of using absolute microbial quantification to better understand, diagnose, and potentially treat SIBO, especially in aging populations. Thank you so much for taking the time to listen to my poster, and be sure to check out the rest of our posters from the MAST program here at DDW. Take care.

answer: Television framing suggests that a golden key, and investor's approval, is the only way a startup can scale. Yet a growing list of multi-million dollar companies share a counterintuitive origin story. Their trajectory only accelerated after their golden opportunity publicly shattered. Over the last decade, business reality television has engineered a very specific cultural myth: the idea that a panel of billionaires possesses a flawless intuition for predicting market winners. The audience is sold a clean, dramatic narrative. A broadcasted handshake equates to instant wealth and market dominance, while a harsh rejection signifies the immediate death of a company. Behind the cameras, the reality of these negotiations is heavily obscured. Real pitches often last anywhere from 45 minutes to two and a half hours, but editors aggressively splice these marathons down into 8-minute segments designed purely for pacing and conflict. The resulting broadcast is a highly engineered media product. It is optimized for entertainment, capturing dramatic confrontations rather than providing a definitive verdict on a company's fundamental market value. The manipulation of the narrative extends beyond the editing bay. A significant percentage of filmed pitches are completely scrapped by producers, meaning many founders endure the entire gauntlet only to never make it to the airwaves. The psychological toll of the process is severe enough that immediately following a rejection, founders are ushered into a room with a show-appointed psychiatrist to evaluate their mental state before they leave the studio. Even for those who survive the pitch and secure a deal, the instantaneous on-screen handshake is largely theatrical. It is immediately followed by months of grueling off-camera due diligence. During that period of intense scrutiny, the most heavily guarded secret of the production comes to light. Roughly two-thirds of the agreements made on television completely collapse in the real world. Consider the case of HyConn. The founder secured a massive 1.25 million dollar agreement on-air, only to see the entire deal evaporate once the camera stopped rolling and the investor decided to aggressively alter the terms of the agreement. Founders are legally prevented from discussing these collapsed deals or leveraging their television appearance to attract other backers because they are bound by strict non-disclosure agreements enforced by the production company. A televised handshake is a flimsy illusion of success. A startup's true test does not happen in the studio. It begins the exact moment the production crew leaves the room. question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Hello everyone, I'm Liangcong from KU Leuven. I'm glad to present our work, Neighbor MAE: Exploiting Spatial Dependencies between Neighboring Earth Observation Images in Masked Autoencoder Pre-training. The main idea of this work is simple. In Earth observation, images are not isolated samples. They are observations of the continuous Earth's surface. So instead of training masked autoencoder on each image independently, we ask whether neighboring images can provide useful spatial context for masked autoencoder pre-training. Masked image modeling has become a popular self-supervised learning strategy for Earth observation. The model masks parts of an image and learns to reconstruct the missing region. However, most existing MIM methods reconstruct a single image tile independently. This is a simplification of Earth observation data because satellite and aerial images are naturally spatially connected. Neighboring images often share useful information, such as terrain structure, land use, continuity, roads, buildings, and infrastructure patterns. At the same time, neighboring views may also differ in acquisition time, viewpoints, or sensor conditions. This means neighboring images provide varied signals, shared spatial context, and natural variations. Therefore, we ask: can neighboring images provide useful context for masked image modeling? To answer this question, we propose Neighbor MAE, which extends MAE from single image reconstruction to joint reconstruction of neighboring Earth observation images. The method has five main components. First, neighbor sampling: we use geospatial metadata to sample neighboring Earth observation images based on the intersection over union of the spatial footprints.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Zero-shot anomaly detection, which aims to detect anomalies in unseen categories, has recently attracted significant attention. In this work, we propose MOE-CLIP: Patch-Specialized Experts for Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection. To perform zero-shot anomaly detection, existing studies primarily use pre-trained CLIP models and apply adapter fine-tuning methods to adapt them to the anomaly detection task. However, conventional approaches process all patches in a monolithic, patch-agnostic manner, without considering the unique characteristics of each patch, such as background patches or anomalous patches. To address this, we propose MOE-CLIP, a mixture-of-experts-based CLIP adaptation method that dynamically selects the most suitable expert for each patch. However, simply applying a mixture-of-experts framework leads to a functional redundancy problem among experts, where multiple experts learn highly similar representations instead of diverse knowledge. Therefore, we further propose FOFS and ETF loss, which encourage each expert to learn distinct and complementary knowledge. Here is the framework of our proposed MOE-CLIP. First, the mixture of LoRA experts module is inserted into the vision encoder layers, enabling dynamic expert selection and adaptation according to the characteristics of each image patch. The approach for achieving expert specialization, FOFS, is a technique applied at the input stage that enforces role separation among experts through the LoRA A matrices. Specifically, it decomposes the input feature space into multiple orthogonal subspaces, forcing each expert to observe only its own unique information without physical overlap with other experts.

answer: I got really good at smiling. So good, that nobody noticed the war happening behind my eyes. I laughed loud, showed up, answered messages with "I'm good". Even cracked jokes while my chest felt like it was carrying a thousand pounds of silence. And the scary part is, after a while, even I started believing the performance. See, depression doesn't always look like darkness. Sometimes it looks like being tired all the time for reasons sleep can't fix. Sometimes it looks like staring at the ceiling at 3:00 a.m. replaying every mistake like your mind signed a contract with regret. Sometimes it sounds like, "You're not enough! You're falling behind! Everybody else figured life out except you!" And you begin to drown in thoughts nobody else can hear. That's the thing about invisible pain. People only notice broken bones, not broken spirits. So you learn survival tricks. You become the therapist friend who secretly needs saving. You become the strong one because strong people aren't allowed to collapse. You disappear into music, into work, into scrolling endlessly at night, hoping distraction feels something like peace. But silence, silence is dangerous. Because when you sit alone long enough, you meet every version of yourself you tried to outrun. The insecure child, the abandoned heart, the exhausted soul. And one day, I realized I wasn't just fighting depression. I was fighting the version of me that believed I had to earn love by suffering quietly. I thought healing meant never hurting again. But healing is actually waking up and choosing to stay, even when your mind tells you to disappear. Healing is messy. It's crying in parked cars, it's canceling plans to breathe, it's admitting, "I'm not okay." before your breaking point introduces you to the ground.

answer: Hi, I'm Chris Avery, I'm the founder of Michaux Media. And this journey for me started back in 2010 while I was deployed to Afghanistan. My mom at the time had sent me a care package, and tucked inside that care package were these stamps featuring this man named Oscar Michaux. Now my mom knew that I had a passion for TV and film, but what she didn't know was that this subtle introduction would drastically change my life. Oscar Michaux lived as a black man during the Great Depression and the segregation of the Jim Crow South. During that time, and despite all of that, he somehow managed to produce, finance, and self-distribute over 40 of his own films entirely independently. He was a maverick who didn't ask for permission. His legacy of self-determination and independence is the absolute inspiration for Michaux Media. Right now, the modern film industry is facing its own unique challenges. Currently, over 85% of the media produced doesn't return its investment, and less than 10% even manages to break even. Hollywood is losing millions because they are bound by outdated production models that fail to engage modern audiences. They are trying to solve a 21st-century problem by gatekeeping 20th-century methods, and it's costing them everything. Michaux Media exists to capture a shift. We want to bet on modern mavericks just like Oscar Michaux. We are building an accelerator platform to de-risk, scale, and monetize creative media before committing massive investment, and shift the power dynamics back to the independent creator. Our platform operates on a four-phase model. First, we host a development sprint designed to test the validity of a project. Second, based on the results of the validation process, we use an internal VC-style model to invest in those ideas that are great and excellent and will go above the mark. And third, we use the most advanced yet financially accessible tools to create proof of concepts. And fourth, we distribute our final result to our pre-vetted and highly curated direct audience. And now is the time for this shift. We are witnessing massive disruption in the entertainment industry. Independent creators are breaking box office records, and we've already seen this in artists like Markiplier and his Iron Lung movie.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: In a world where we do almost everything on screens, you might wonder: Does it really matter whether we journal digitally or on paper? Surprisingly, it does. Writing in a paper journal can actually be far more powerful for healing, self-awareness, and changing behavior than typing on a screen. In this video, I'm going to explain why writing by hand can create deeper emotional clarity and lasting personal change. Writing by hand engages the brain more deeply. When you write on paper, your brain works differently than when you type. Handwriting activates multiple parts of the brain related to memory, emotion, and learning. Typing tends to be fast and automatic. But writing by hand slows your thinking down. That slower pace allows you to process your thoughts more carefully, which helps you understand your emotions and experiences more clearly. In other words, handwriting helps your brain move from reacting to reflecting. Slowing down creates emotional awareness. Healing starts with awareness. When you journal on paper, the natural rhythm of writing encourages you to slow down and become more aware of what you are feeling. Instead of quickly typing and moving on, you begin to notice your emotions, your thoughts, your reactions, and the patterns in your behavior. This moment of pause is incredibly powerful because you cannot change what you are not aware of. Paper feels more private and honest. A physical journal often feels safer than digital writing. It isn't connected to the internet. There are no notifications, no audience, no distractions. Because of that, many people feel more comfortable writing honestly about things like fears, regrets, anger, sadness, or uncertainty. And that honesty is essential for healing. Your journal becomes a place where you can tell the truth without being judged. The physical act of writing releases emotion. There's also something deeply therapeutic about the physical act of writing itself. The movement of pen on paper can feel grounding and calming. When emotions feel overwhelming, writing them out physically can help release that tension. Many people notice that after writing honestly about something difficult, they feel lighter, calmer, clearer. Sometimes, the page holds emotions that were too heavy to carry alone. Your journal becomes a record of growth. One of the most powerful aspects of paper journaling is that you can see your journey over time.

answer: There was a point in time, earlier on in my spiritual awakening journey, when I was concerned with growth and getting better. Not that I don't want to grow now because of course I do, but in the beginning, the pursuit of growth was all-consuming. It was ego-driven. I went to the gym regularly, I meditated, I read self-help, spiritual books, and took notes. I even took up coaching others in an attempt to ditch the nine-to-five scene. None of the habits stuck for more than a few months, but I would always come back to them the following year. Like I said, it was ego-driven. I wanted to do better because, deep down, I felt I wasn't good enough. I felt behind in life, like I should be further along. And although that way of pursuing growth and self-improvement served its purpose, I now understand it's not the best way. Actually, I would even go as far as to say as adding habits to your daily routine for the sole purpose of getting better is the very thing that keeps you from getting better. Often times, our pursuit for better is rooted in social validation. We want to be liked, we want to be accepted, we want to be seen in a particular light. And the problem doesn't come from not being noticed or liked. Often times, along these sorts of external focus journeys, we are seen and liked, but we aren't seen and liked for who we actually are. I believe a better way to improve oneself is not to download a bunch of habits influencers have said that have changed their lives, but to do more of the things you enjoy. Lean into yourself, and forget what the internet says is good or bad. If running is what you love, then run because you love it, not because you think in three months you'll be a different person. If you genuine- if you genuinely enjoy having a couple of beers at the end of the day, have a couple of beers. The biggest lie the self-improvement space sold us was that there's something wrong with who we are, and that we need to fix it. There is nothing wrong with who you are or where you are at in life. We are all walking our own paths, evolving at our own pace. Don't let a stranger on the internet make you feel less than you are. True and lasting change will come when you're ready. And when you're ready, the change will be effortless. Trust your journey. It was carved for you. Thank you for watching. Have a good day.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: We live our days as if we have an endless supply of tomorrows. But every spring here in Japan, the cherry blossoms remind us of a truth we often try to ignore. A beautiful life isn't one that lasts forever. It is one that blooms fully before the wind takes it away. Every spring, the entire country stops to watch the sakura open. People gather under the trees, lay out blankets, and share food, tea, and be happy together. It's a tradition called Hanami. But if you've never experienced this exact thing in your life, you might not realize what makes the sakura so deeply connected to how we experience life. They only bloom for about 10 to 14 days, sometimes even less. A single strong wind or an early heavy rain can take them all away in one night. And that is exactly why they are so beautiful. If cherry blossoms stayed on the trees forever, nobody would stop to look at them. Since everyone sitting under those trees knows that this moment will not last, they pay attention. They just sit there and soak it in, feeling a deep stillness, aware that the petals are already falling. When I was younger, I used to live as if time was unlimited. I would waste entire days doing things I didn't care about. I would stay in situations that made me unhappy, telling myself I'd change things later. I felt this constant pressure to do everything faster and achieve more, while consistently postponing the things I truly wanted to do. This truth about time really hit me when my grandfather, Daiki, passed away. It happened so quickly that one season, he was sitting with me in his garden, pouring tea and telling me stories. And the next season, his chair was empty, like a petal falling from a branch. After he passed, I was going through his things and found an old journal entry he had written during his last spring. I carry his words with me every single day. He wrote, "Hiroto, the real tragedy of life is how many of our years we waste. The sakura never worries about tomorrow's wind."

Planning for modularity reduces both long-term costs and the environmental footprint of constant tech replacement. Not every event requires brand-new technology. Many attendees care far more about meaningful content and clear audiovisual output than the generation of the device being used.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: Have you ever been lying awake at 2:00 a.m. feeling a physical weight in your chest while your mind races through a tornado of unfinished tasks, looming deadlines and vague anxieties? That sensation signals a specific biological chain reaction taking place in your nervous system. When you perceive a threat, even something as small as a tense email, your brain's threat detection center, the amygdala, fires an alarm and floods your system with cortisol. If this stress stays chronic, neuroimaging shows that your amygdala actually grows larger and more reactive, while your prefrontal cortex, the area responsible for rational executive planning, shrinks and effectively goes offline. To break this cycle, you need a mechanism called cognitive diffusion. By taking those chaotic, swirling thoughts out of your head and translating them into physical words on a page, you force your rational prefrontal cortex to re-engage, which physically turns down the amygdala's alarm system. The worry dump is a structured, analog practice designed to create this distance. It requires putting pen to paper to begin the process of externalization. Grab a physical pen, a piece of paper, and a timer. We are going to walk through this exact process together right now. Moving thoughts onto paper provides a physiological intervention to stall cortisol and reclaim your cognitive control. Step one is to find a quiet, private space where you will not be interrupted. You need an environment where your analytical left brain can focus on the physical act of writing, giving your creative right brain the safety to wander and release everything it's holding onto. Set your timer for exactly five minutes. When it starts, your only job is to write down every single worry, task, and anxious thought currently occupying your mind. Here is the single most critical rule for this phase: you must write continuously. Do not pause to organize your thoughts. Do not prioritize the list. And do not stop to analyze why you are stressed about a certain item. Ignore your inner critic. If you stop to correct your spelling or fix your grammar, you will pull yourself out of the flow and stall the exercise. Keep your pen moving. If your mind suddenly goes blank and you run out of things to say, simply rewrite your last sentence over and over again until a new thought emerges, or until the timer officially sounds. Your output does not need to make sense to anyone else. A single word, a fragmented phrase, or a complete sentence are all equally valid forms of output. Just get it on the page.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: You ever notice how some people look completely fine on the outside? But something about them feels tired? Not physically tired. Soul tired. They wake up, go to work, answer texts, laugh at the right moments, pay bills, scroll their phone at night, and repeat the same cycle over and over again like a machine pretending to be a human being. And nobody notices because nothing is technically wrong. That's the terrifying part. Quiet desperation doesn't always look like a breakdown. Sometimes it looks like functioning perfectly while slowly dying inside. Henry David Thoreau once wrote that most men live lives of quiet desperation, and the older I get, the more disturbing that sentence becomes. Because desperation is easy to recognize when it's loud. When someone's screaming, spiraling, crashing out, everybody sees it. But quiet desperation, that hides behind routines, behind careers, behind relationships, behind smiling photos, and "I'm good" responses. It's the kind of suffering that learns how to behave, and I think a lot of people fall into it without even realizing it. It starts with tiny compromises, tiny betrayals of yourself. "I'll chase my dream later." "I'll settle for this job for now." "I'll stay in this relationship because at least it's familiar." And at first, it feels temporary, but temporary has a way of becoming permanent when fear gets comfortable. Years pass. Your responsibilities grow roots around you, and one day you wake up realizing you built an entire life around survival, but forgot to include yourself in it. That's why some people feel empty even after getting everything they thought they wanted. Because achievement without alignment creates exhaustion. You can win the game and still hate waking up in the morning. You can make money and still feel spiritually bankrupt. You can be surrounded by people and still feel emotionally isolated. Quiet desperation is the gap between the life you're living and the life your soul knows you were meant for. And social media makes it worse. Now everybody performs happiness like it's a full-time job. People don't even ask, "Am I fulfilled anymore?" They ask, "Do I look fulfilled?"

answer: Football could be on the brink of its biggest civil war in decades. UEFA has just issued one of the strongest statements we've ever seen against FIFA. The World Cup is not for sale. According to UEFA, football's greatest competition should never become an investment product for private shareholders. The organization says the World Cup belongs to players, national teams and supporters across generations, not investors looking for financial returns. And UEFA wasn't just angry about the proposal itself. It also criticized the way FIFA handled the entire process. According to the statement, such an important decision was developed behind closed doors and brought close to approval without meaningful consultation with the people responsible for governing the sport. That criticism goes beyond business. It's about trust. UEFA believes decisions that shape football's future should involve open discussions with confederations, leagues, clubs and national associations. Instead, it believes FIFA acted alone.

answer: This assistant answers questions from 300 podcast episodes. Watch what happens when I ask it something those episodes don't cover. It refuses. That refusal is the hardest thing in this project, and it isn't a prompt instruction, it's enforced in code. Lenny's Podcast is hundreds of interviews with product and growth leaders. The insight you need is in there, but it is scattered. A question like, "How do I know I have product market fit?" gets answered by a dozen guests who disagree with each other. Search gives you fragments. A general chatbot gives you a fluent answer with invented attribution. I wanted both synthesis and sources. Still on the local model, it retrieves from Postgres using hybrid search, vector similarity fused with full-text ranking, and then answers only from what came back. Every claim carries a bracket, and every bracket resolves to a real episode and a named guest. If it can't cite it, it doesn't say it. A cloud model will follow an instruction like "only use these excerpts." A 1-billion-parameter local model won't. Asked that cooking question, it answered from its own memory and attached a citation to an unrelated excerpt so the answer looked sourced. So, scope became code. These rules only ever see the retrieval evidence, never your question, which means they can't quietly turn into a banned topic list. Three cheaper approaches failed first. I even asked the model to judge its own grounding. Two out of six, and in one case, it answered, "Yes, this is answerable," while its own reason said the excerpt didn't discuss the topic. There are four skills, and a three-tier router decides which one runs. Cheap pattern matching goes first. "Build me a dashboard" never needs a model call at all. Only genuinely ambiguous requests reach the LLM classifier, and that classifier also rewrites the search query because a conversational question makes a poor embedding. You can watch it decide in the logs: the skill, the tier, the confidence, and then the retrieval fan-out underneath. The second skill writes "Ship 30 for 30" essays: strong hook, short paragraphs, bolded phrases so it can be skimmed, a clear takeaway at the end, and citations running through it. This one measured at 1,301 words against a 1,250-word target, nine bold phrases, 10 bullets, five sources. The third skill generates artifacts. The design system comes from the app, and things like an empty table or a mismatched column count get repaired in code. So, a small model can produce a thin page, but not a broken one. Now that you have your journal notebook created, you can start thinking about how to organize your entries effectively. There, you will see an option to create a "new subnotebook." For starters, you might want to create a subnotebook titled "Daily entries." This section will be where you jot down your thoughts and reflections every day. It's a space for freeform writing, capturing everything from daily events to personal reflections. Next, consider adding a subnotebook for "Weekly reviews." This section is great for reflecting on the week that just passed. It offers a valuable opportunity to see how your thoughts and experiences have evolved over the past seven days, and help set intentions for the following week. Finally, there's the "Monthly reviews" subnotebook. Monthly reviews are vital for looking at the bigger picture. They allow you to track longer-term goals and assess progress over time. Reflecting monthly provides a macro perspective of your life, habits, and achievements. When you envision this structure in Joplin, it might look like a tree, with "Journal" as the trunk, "Daily entries," "Weekly reviews," and "Monthly reviews" act as the branches extending from it, providing a clear pathway for your thoughts to spread. By organizing your journal in this manner, you create a harmonious and systematic approach that enhances your journaling practice. This customized structure caters to different aspects of life reflection, and makes it simpler for you to navigate through your thoughts and feelings. Once everything is set up, you can start using Joplin to capture your life's details, review your growth, and make journaling an enriching experience.

question: Transcribe the audio to text
answer: A bill introduced in parliament on Friday could fundamentally change who the Indian state recognizes as transgender and who it doesn't. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill 2026 was tabled in the Lok Sabha by Social Justice Minister Virendra Kumar. And while the government says it's about bringing clarity to a vague law, critics say it could quietly dismantle rights that took years of struggle to win. I'm Vrinda Tulsian and you're watching The Print. To understand what's changed and why it matters, we need to go back to where this all began. It's 2014. The Supreme Court delivers what becomes known as the NALSA judgment, a landmark ruling that recognizes transgender persons as a third gender, directs the government to provide reservations and welfare measures, and crucially holds that a person has the right to self-identify their gender, no surgery required, no medical certificate, no government approval. The court said the constitution guarantees it. That judgment set the stage for legislation, but getting a law passed took five more years, and they weren't smooth years. A 2016 version of the bill was met with protest from the transgender communities across the country. The core objection: it required a District Magistrate to certify whether someone was transgender. Activists said that handed a bureaucrat the power to decide something the Supreme Court had said was a fundamental right. After sustained pressure, the bill was revised. The Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was finally passed in 2019. It was imperfect, many in the community still had reservations, but it represented a floor, a legal baseline. It defined transgender persons broadly: anyone whose gender doesn't match the gender assigned at birth, including trans men, trans women, genderqueer individuals, those with intersex variations, and those with socio-cultural identities like hijra, kinnar, aravani, and jogta, and it explicitly said, under Section 4, Part 2, that a recognized transgender person has the right to a self-perceived gender identity. That section is now proposed to be deleted. So what exactly does the 2026 amendment propose? There are three major changes worth unpacking: the definition, the procedures, and the penalties. Under the new bill, the term transgender person would be restricted to two categories: first, people with specific socio-cultural identities—hijra, kinnar, aravani, jogta, eunuch—or people born with medically recognized intersex variations. Variations in chromosomes, genitalia, hormones, gonadal development, biological markers, in other words.
